title: Barge In
pitch: A human and an AI drawing on the same canvas — and the page can say no.
about_excerpt: A human and an AI drawing on the same canvas — and the page can say no. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most WebMCP demos hand an agent tools that read the page. I wanted to hand it tools that touch something a person is touching at the same time, and see what breaks. Everything broke immediately, and in an interesting way. In the first experiment a human drew seven strokes across the agent's work-in-progress. The agent never noticed. Not a bug — WebMCP is pull-only. A page cannot speak to its agent. It has no notify , no event, no way up the pipe. It can only answer when it is called. So the question became: with only that one channel, how much control can a page take back? What it does The page gives an agent nine drawing tools. Ask it for a lion; it draws one. Then pick up the mouse and draw two wheels underneath it while it works. 19:18:40 You Drew a line (9 points) ← you barge in mid-batch … You × 7 more 19:18:48 AI ⛔ Blocked canvas_batch — canvas changed by human 19:18:48 AI Inspected the updated canvas 19:19:02 AI Updated the plan — A cute smiling male lion car, using the completed red user-drawn wheels and connecting them to the mane-body with a simple axle. 19:19:12 AI Drew 39 shapes in one batch Its half-finished mane stops where it stopped, because the rest of that batch was dropped . It cannot draw again until it has looked, and then said what your wheels changed about the plan — and what it is giving up because of them. In this run it said, unprompted: "Both red wheels now have hubs, inner rims, and tread marks. I'll keep those wheel details untouched and add only the axle connection." Then it drew the axle. Not a lion that happens to still have wheels beside it — a lion joined to your wheels by a bar it decided to add. About sixty seconds, start to finish, with nothing scripted anywhere. Every one of those decisions came out of the agent reading tool output. The drawing is deliberately crude. An image model would draw a better lion. The log is the deliverable. How I built it First, a word on what this is not . WebMCP already has a human-in-the-loop hook — requestUserInteraction , which lets a tool pause and ask the person to confirm. That is agent-initiated : the agent decides to ask, the person waits in front of a dialog, and says yes or no to something already drafted. It is consent. This is the opposite shape. It is human-initiated : the person acts whenever they like, without asking, and the agent finds out afterwards that it has been overruled. It is pre-emption. Both belong in a page people and agents share, and the spec currently offers only the first. Someone who is making something does not want to approve the agent's plan — they want to reach in and change it, and have the agent catch up. Then four rules, each one arrived at by watching the previous version fail. 1 — Refuse, don't stop. A page cannot interrupt an agent. But an agent calls a tool every few seconds, so refusing the next call feels, to the person watching, like an instant stop. Every writing tool calls guard() first. 2 — If you cannot push, answer when you are pulled. Everything the page needs to say rides back on the tool the agent already calls. canvas_describe always appends what the human did since the last check. It is the only channel WebMCP offers, so the page uses it as one. 3 — Seeing is not accepting. The first version asked , in prose, for the agent to re-plan around the interruption. It obliged — narrated the change beautifully, then carried on drawing its original picture. So looking stopped being enough: canvas_describe now hands over to a second gate, and only canvas_replan(observed, new_plan, abandoning) opens it. All three fields are required. abandoning is the load-bearing one — a plan you have given nothing up for is the old plan wearing a new sentence. 4 — The human's marks are never painted over. Told to incorporate the wheels, the agent laid its mane straight over them. Nothing was deleted and the counts were honest, but half the wheels vanished from the picture, and the picture is what people read. Paint order is now fixed: whatever the agent draws goes underneath. Challenges I ran into Requests land; prohibitions do not. "Check the canvas before you draw" was ignored, however it was worded. Refusing the call was not. Every rule here is enforced by a code path, not by asking nicely. Batching fixed the speed and broke the premise. A realistic lion took six minutes — the agent called canvas_stroke with three points every four seconds. Adding canvas_batch cut it to one call . The next tester's report was one sentence: "It drew everything at once, so I had no time to barge in." Painting the batch slowly to look interruptible would have been a lie — the picture was already decided. So a batch is now accepted and laid down one shape at a time over a few seconds, and if the human draws during that, the rest is dropped and never happens. Batching gained an honest price: bigger is faster, and bigger loses more. The agent answers in the conversation's language. Asked in Japanese, it wrote its new plan in Japanese, onto an English canvas. Fixed by asking for English in three places — the tool description, each parameter's description, and the return value read immediately before the call. One place was not enough. Accomplishments I'm proud of The measured finding that surprised me most has nothing to do with drawing: A tool's description changes how an agent batches its work. With a neutral description, the agent drew a spiral as 2 points per call, ~40 calls, over a minute. After adding "Pass every point in one call. Each call costs a few seconds, so the number of calls is the wait the user sees" — 121 points in a single call, in 4 seconds. Same tool, same model, 15× fewer round trips, from one paragraph of prose. What I learned That a page under WebMCP is not a passive surface. It is the only party in the room that knows what the person just did, and the return value of a tool is a real communication channel — one the agent reads carefully and acts on. Almost all the design work turned out to be writing. What's next The mechanism is now a standalone file, barge-in.js , that knows nothing about drawing. It knows only who touched the page last, and it is four lines to add to a page: const bi = BargeIn.create({ describeTool: 'doc_read', replanTool: 'doc_replan' }); editor.addEventListener('input', () => { bi.note('you', 'edited a paragraph'); // look() reports this bi.humanActed(); // this refuses the agent }); function doc_insert(p) { bi.guard(); /* … */ } // guard every write function doc_read() { return Object.assign({ text: editor.value }, bi.look()); } The first application already runs, as a second page in the same repo: examples/doc.html , a document a person and an agent write at the same time — six tools, the same barge-in.js behind them, about 250 lines of page on top. video_transcript_excerpt: An AI was drawing. You took the mouse. Its next tool call was refused. And it stays refused until it looks again and tells you what changed. Nothing here is scripted. The page simply refuses. WebMCP is pull only. A page cannot speak to its agent. It can only answer when it is called. So, every mechanism here is built from the one channel that exists, what a tool returns. Watch. One call, not 60. You barge in. The rest of that batch is dropped. It never happens. It looks again. It writes its own new plan. A lion car. The wheels connected by an axle. Then it draws the axle. Your wheels are still on top. They always are. Fetch home news twins. Wells down stalker does tapering via answer phones of survival. The drawing is deliberately crude. An image model would draw a better lion. This log is the deliverable. Four rules. Refuse. Don't stop. A page cannot interrupt an agent, but it can refuse its next call. If you cannot push, hand it over the next time you are pulled. Seeing is not accepting. Drawing stays locked until it declares a new plan and what it is dropping. And the humans marks are never painted over. live_observation.first_impression: A canvas experiment page presents drawing controls, colors, tools, a call log, and a WebMCP status button.
live_observation.after_state: The Line tool remained available, but no visible canvas change or call-log entry appeared from the click alone.
live_observation.notes: The page loaded normally; the central drawing workflow appears to require canvas pointer input or agent calls.
